Covid19 and Waste Water

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With a Covid-19 vaccine still months from being a reality, could our waste water systems prove to be the ultimate early warning systems for detecting viral loads in South African communities?

Unique Selling Point:
The South African waste water treatment system is in a state of disaster - but according to Professor Anthony Turton the current Covid19 pandemic might just present the perfect opportunity, created by the perfect storm. Using new technology already available in the Netherlands, we could use our waste water treatment plants to detect Covid 19 viral loads in South Africans - and the best part is international funding is available to kickstart the project, which could see the first testing happen within a month, if the SA Government buys into the idea. The relatively small investment in setting up the systems would offer many benefits - it would be cheaper than trying to test the almost 59 million individuals in South Africa, and would mean we could do continuous testing on high density populations - something that will not be possible with individuals. Meanwhile, while Covid19 is found in human faeaces, the jury is still out on whether it can be transmitted in this way. But experts warn it's better to be safe than sorry.

Summary:
Using waste water treatment plants to test for substances ingested by humans is not new technology - the FBI uses it in America to screen large populations for overall drug use, and are able to successfully see if there are spikes in drug intakes in certain areas. The same technology can be used to test for Covid 19 - by testing waste water coming into treatment plants before it is chemically treated. This would allow for large scale analysis of dense populations, like the urban metropols mostly affected by the disease in SA. But our current waste water treatment system is in a state of complete chaos - could the covid19 crisis be the critical turning point in preventing an even larger public health crisis, the collapse of our national water systems.

Further information:
We have identified top experts to deliver commentary

We have footage available from previous stories on waste water disasters around the country

We have footage available on the new technology

We will travel to Hartebeespoort Dam to film the current situation of raw sewage spilling onto the streets, into people's homes and into the dam.

We will follow the water system from the dam to farms where untreated water is pumped onto crops

We will speak to epidemiologists on the implications of Covid 19 in faeces.

Press Release:


COVID-19 in Wastewater – Early Warning of Infection?
With the virus that causes COVID-19 found in the stool of some patients treated for the disease, scientists are investigating whether wastewater in sewage systems is a sure signal that the disease has spread. Carte Blanche investigates whether the presence of COVID-19 in our wastewater systems could serve as an early warning system of imminent outbreak and asks whether South Africa’s rundown municipal sewage systems pose a risk of infection to nearby residents.
Producer: Graham Coetzer | Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:


Covid-19 & Waste Water
First Draft Script
29 April 2020


Voice
South Africa is moving into a phased easing of the national lockdown. For the plan to work successfully, we’ll have to constantly monitor the local transmission rate of the deadly Covid-19 virus. But in a country of 59 million people, how do we determine who to test?

Link Masa
With a vaccine still months in the making and no cure insight, large scale testing will be crucial in South Africa’s fight to curb rising numbers of Covid-19 infections. But an innovative solution could be on the horizon - one that could cancel the need to test millions of individuals.

Voice
The answers might come from the very last place you’d expect to find them - our toilets. That’s because traces of the Corona virus can be found in stool samples of infected people, and therefore also in our sewage. In a process called Waste Water Epideemiology, scientists are able to;

-collect samples of waste water coming into a sewage works,

-test those samples for Covid-19

-and analyse the data to track the spread of the virus.

Because it is known which suburbs feed into which sewage plants, scientists can use the data to accurately model levels of infections across the country, without having to test thousands of indivduals.

Professor Wolfgang Prizer is the head of Medical Virology at the University of Stellenbosch.

Sound Up Prof Wolgang Presier
So this is quite an interesting tool, and it has been applied for virology. So people have looked in waste water to see what viruses infect the population that feeds these waste water streams.

Voice
Frederic Been is a researcher from the KWR water research institute in the Netherlands. he says the institute has successfully applied the technique in his home country.

Sound Up Frederic Been
Masa: Tell us about this innovative solution to be able to bridge waste water, with the fight against Covid-19. How can we merge these tow and can they work together when it comes to testing for instance.

Frederic: From waste water you can gather a lot of information about the public, the health status and the lifestyle of people. So if you collect waste water at the entrance of a waste water treatment plant, and you collect samples, and you analyse for the genetic material of the virus in these samples, you can actually know whether it’s present in that community.

Voice
Been and his team have managed to find traces of Covid-19 in sewage, before patients presented at hospitals with symptoms of the virus. It’s a powerful early warning tool for authorities.

Sound Up Frederic
People that do not present symptoms, or have mild symptoms, might not get tested, so you have this dark number, or hidden number of how many people are actually infected.

Voice
Benoit le Roy is the co founder of the South African Water Chamber, and says the technology could be a game changer in countries like South Africa that are struggling with testing capacity.

Sound Up Benoit
So from a South African perspective, where we have far less resources, we would be able to track the movement of the virus and infections even before the outbreaks are actually picked up.

Link Masa
It by no means is new technology, law enforcement agencies across the globe have already been monitoring waste water in the same way. They’ve been collecting the data for use in a whole other war, the war on drugs.

Voice
In countries like China, the USA and across Europe, officials use waste water epidemiology to monitor illegal drug usage. This allows law enforcement to not only identify which drugs are being consumed, but also to target dealers, in areas where the market is suddenly flooded with certain drugs.

Sound Up Wolfgang
People can look in waste water for cases of drugs. Illicit drugs or medical compounds and they can see what the population that feeds these wastewater streams, what they are using.

Voice
With indivdual Covid-19 tests, authorities only get results for a single person at a given time. They won’t know if that person gets infected two days later. Using Waste Water Epidemiology, they could test tens of thousands of people at regular timed intervals. And by analysing the amount of virus present in the samples, make informed decisions on which areas of the population are most at risk.

Sound Up Frederic Been
Of course if the amount of virus in waste water decreases, or increases, this is an image of what’s actually happening in the population. So are more, or less people infected. So you can follow the circulation of the virus in the population by analysing it’s waste water.

Voice
Experts say the virus is mainly transmitted through large respiratory droplets expelled when people cough or sneeze. But a number of researchers are concerned about the aerosols, or fine liquid droplets, that are released at the same time. Doctor Jo Barnes is an epidemiologist and senior lecturer at the university of Stellenbosch who specialises in Communitiy Health.

Sound Up Jo Barnes
The tiny droplets, are very light, and they float in the air, for a number of hours. And it seems as if the people who are vulnerable, when they inhale that, they inhale enough virus to make some of them ill.

Voice
Aerosolization also occurs when you flush your toilet, as moving water and air mix. No studies have yet proven that the virus can be transmitted this way, but in any case it’s good hygiene practice to close the lid and disinfect regularly.

Sound Up Professor Barnes
There are other pathogens that will make people ill in sewage, that are equally dangerous, but we now have an added one, called the corona virus.

Voice
But the risk of transmission by flushing is minor compared to what many South Africans are exposed to daily.


Link Masa
We’ve just arrived in Hartebeespoort, where scenes like this, of raw sewage streaming down the streets, are an all too common occurrence.

Voice
The Madibeng municipality is currently under administration, but the intervention has not helped the locals, says ward councillor and resident Erna Rossouw.

Sound Up Erna Rossouw
So it’s going around the corner into the storm water drain and then straight to the Hartebeespoort dam. And the smell is awful.

Voice
Just a few kilometers down the road is the small community of Refentse, where resident Tshepo Chabalala is dealing with the same problem - in his backyard.

Sound Up Tshepo
Masa: Tell me about what I am seeing here? All this water here, what is it? Is it sewage?
Tshepo: It is sewage which is full and overflowing. So when we call the municipality office they tell us that the municipality has no money. There is nothing that the municipality can do.
Voice
Chabalala says an already unbearable situation has been exacerbated by the national lockdown

Sound Up Thsepo
Masa: Where are the children playing when it’s like this?

Tshepo: There is no space for the children to play, the children always stay inside the house because there is no… When they go outside they might also be affected by this sewage.

Voice
Professor Presier says that having the public in contact with raw sewage like this is a serious health hazard.
Sound Up Wolfgang
That virus is not that hardy that it should survive proper sewage treatment. Now of course, informal settlements, where sewage may run down the streets, and where others may be exposed to it, by playing in it, kids, that is of course a potential worry, and that is not a good situation.

Voice
The Birdwood Estate, also in Hartebeespoort, is an upmarket development that offers exquisite views of the dam - but the pump station along it’s borders is currently out of order - Leaking sewage along the estate’s boundary wall. Estate manager Ronaldo Bettini says it has a knock on effect on their whole sewer system.

Sound Up Ronaldo
Ronaldo: So it starts blowing up in the showers, and in the toilets in the private properties here.
Masa: Wait, sewage in the showers and the toilets?
Ronaldo: In the showers and the toilets.
Masa: So I’ll be in the shower, and then from nowhere, sewage?
Ronaldo: Correct.
Masa: And that is the experience of residents here?
Ronaldo: That’s the residents. That’s what they’re sitting with here for the past three years now already.
Voice
In their response, the Madibeng Municipality said that temporary conservancy tanks it installed at the Refentse settlement to manage waste water drainage, had failed. “These conservancy tanks were not constructed to the correct standard and have since largely collapsed. The re-construction of the tanks to the correct standard now forms part of the list of projects approved…” They also said that the blocked drain had been fixed, and… “Concerning raw sewage noted along Birdwood estate, the Zanadu pump station was reported to have a level sensor challenge, which has since been resolved.”
Anthony Turton is a professor at the Centre for Environmental Management at the university of the Free State, and says it’s a nationwide problem.
Sound Up Anthony Turton
And I described it as a train smash, that’s happening while we watch.
Voice
And he’s warned government that the failing municipal water infrastructure around the country is a slow onset disaster.
Sound Up Anthony
So a slow onset disaster is something that we know with a very high level of confidence what the end result will be, but for some reason we don’t seem to be able to convey that urgency through to the relevant authorities.

Voice
Hopefully it’s a problem that will be addressed by President Ramaphosa’s relief plan for municipalities during the pandemic. But what does that mean for techniques like waste water epideemiology?

Link Masa
It makes sense, in theory. But in a country where our waste water treatment plants are already in dire straights, could it really work?

Sound Up Benoit
Benoit: Well,if you have a look at our sewage system, whether it’s working or not, the sewage is going to the sewage works, is the first thing. And the sampling is done at what we call the head of the works, so before we do any treatment or not.

Voice
And that’s good news, especially since it won’t cost all that much to implement. Le Roy says it’s more about the knowledge being made available from institutes like KWR, than massive infrastructure upgrades. And if government decides to implement the technology here in South Africa, we could see our first results a month later.

Sound Up Benoit
You know you don’t have to import anything except the knowledge of actually putting those protocols together, because our laboratories in the world and in South Africa included are all able to do those tests.













Promo 1
Voice
In the US, law enforcement agencies test sewage water to determine which areas are drug hotzones - Can scientists in South Africa use the same techniques to track the deadly Covid-19 virus?

Promo 2
Voice
By testing our sewage for Covid-19, scientists could predict in which areas of South Africa we can expect to find large groups of infected people - even before they start showing symptoms.

Promo 3
Voice
Innovative techniques are allowing scientists to track Covid-19 outbreaks in the last place you’d expect to find it - our sewage. Could the technology help flatten the curve in South Africa?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): With a Covid-19 vaccine still months from being a reality, could our waste water systems prove to be the ultimate early warning systems for detecting viral loads in South African communities?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The South African waste water treatment system is in a state of disaster - but according to Professor Anthony Turton the current Covid19 pandemic might just present the perfect opportunity, created by the perfect storm. Using new technology already available in the Netherlands, we could use our waste water treatment plants to detect Covid 19 viral loads in South Africans - and the best part is international funding is available to kickstart the project, which could see the first testing happen within a month, if the SA Government buys into the idea. The relatively small investment in setting up the systems would offer many benefits - it would be cheaper than trying to test the almost 59 million individuals in South Africa, and would mean we could do continuous testing on high density populations - something that will not be possible with individuals. Meanwhile, while Covid19 is found in human faeaces, the jury is still out on whether it can be transmitted in this way. But experts warn it's better to be safe than sorry.
metadata.Summary: Using waste water treatment plants to test for substances ingested by humans is not new technology - the FBI uses it in America to screen large populations for overall drug use, and are able to successfully see if there are spikes in drug intakes in certain areas. The same technology can be used to test for Covid 19 - by testing waste water coming into treatment plants before it is chemically treated. This would allow for large scale analysis of dense populations, like the urban metropols mostly affected by the disease in SA. But our current waste water treatment system is in a state of complete chaos - could the covid19 crisis be the critical turning point in preventing an even larger public health crisis, the collapse of our national water systems.
metadata.Further information: We have identified top experts to deliver commentary We have footage available from previous stories on waste water disasters around the country We have footage available on the new technology We will travel to Hartebeespoort Dam to film the current situation of raw sewage spilling onto the streets, into people's homes and into the dam. We will follow the water system from the dam to farms where untreated water is pumped onto crops We will speak to epidemiologists on the implications of Covid 19 in faeces.
